Bigger local budgets, thin local capacity

Local governments got far more money than they could plan and spend. The fix: hand over functions at the pace of readiness.

See the proposalRead the issue
₱959.04 billionNational Tax Allotment in FY 2022, a 37.89 percent rise over the FY 2021 shares (DBM, 2021).

The short version

The problem

Local budgets rose 37.89 percent after the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, but many LGUs could not plan, staff and buy at that scale.

The answer

Use EO 103's phased deadlines as the base. Add milestone-based fund releases and province-anchored shared staff.

The test

Six indicators, reviewed every year until FY 2028 and reported by income class.

Core 1 of 5Globalization driver

Globalization driverDevelopment

Global decentralization models and the Sustainable Development Goals raise what local governments are expected to deliver, and the OECD sees decentralization as especially important for places left behind by globalization (OECD, 2019).

This site treats the driver as a framing influence, not outside pressure, since national agencies and LGUs still decide what actually happens. It is also what the Driver alignment score measures: how directly a solution answers the gap between what these models expect of LGUs and what LGUs can deliver.

Source: Week 8 Worksheet and MS2 Essay, Actors and Perspectives and Table 2.

Core 2 of 5Current status

Where things stand now.

The original FY 2024 deadline has passed. The handover is still unfinished, and the money keeps arriving faster than many LGUs can use it.

Current status 1

The clock was reset

On November 6, 2025, EO 103 extended the transition. Deadlines now run to FY 2027 for cities and FY 2028 for provinces and municipalities, tied to what each LGU can handle, with priority for poorer localities (Hufana, 2025; Romero, 2025).

Current status 2

Reliance is still heavy

Transfers made up 84 percent of municipal income on average in 2018, and 98 percent in poorer areas (Juco et al., 2026). PIDS reported in June 2026 that devolution remains incomplete despite higher funding (Juco et al., 2026; Manila Bulletin Newsroom, 2026).

Current status 3

Help is still early

DILG Region XI briefed its field officers on EO 103 in June 2026 (DILG Region XI, 2026). I found no report yet of capacity building or funds reaching the 4th and 5th class LGUs the order prioritizes. DBM confirmed in March 2026 that the Growth Equity Fund continues (DBM, 2026).

Source: the news timeline and the Limits note on this page. The P155 billion unspent figure is a World Bank forecast and not a result ("WB Worried," 2021).

The whole argument in five steps

LGU: a local government unit, meaning a province, city, municipality or barangay. EO 103: the 2025 order that amended EO 138 and set new, phased deadlines for devolving national functions to LGUs. Mandanas-Garcia ruling: the Supreme Court decision that computes the LGU share from all national taxes.

1 · The problem

Money outran capacity

37.89%

Local budgets rose 37.89 percent (DBM, 2021), but many LGUs could not plan, staff and buy at that scale. Funding and capacity are two separate constraints.

Section 1 → 2 · The disagreement

Agencies split on the pace

DBM wants full handover, gradually. DILG, LGUs, PIDS and the World Bank want capacity in place before functions move down.

Section 2 → 3 · The options

Three solutions, one winner

EO 103 phased devolution scored highest at 3.4 of 4, ahead of the Growth Equity Fund (2.8) and inter-LGU alliances (2.4).

Section 5 → 4 · The proposal

EO 103 plus two add-ons

DBM, the Bureau of the Treasury and the steering committee release Growth Equity Fund money against capacity milestones, and let provinces anchor shared professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff.

Section 6 → 5 · The test

Six indicators

Reviewed every year until FY 2028 and reported by income class, so progress is judged by results.

Section 1 of 9 · Source: Worksheet and Essay

Understanding the Issue

What the Mandanas-Garcia ruling changed, why many LGUs could not use the larger budgets, and how the problem is defined.

Money arrived faster than capacity.

A local government unit (LGU) is a province, city, municipality or barangay. The ruling gave them far more to spend before many could plan and buy at that scale.

Focus and position

Focus issue

Local fiscal decentralization and administrative absorptive capacity

Under the Mandanas-Garcia ruling, LGUs gained far more money than many could plan, staff and buy for.

My position

Pace devolution by readiness

More local funding respects LGU autonomy, but forcing full devolution faster than LGUs can build administrative and procurement capacity weakens services and could widen the gap between better-resourced and lower-income LGUs. Extra help should go to the LGUs that need it most.

Source: Week 8 Worksheet and MS2 Essay, Introduction.

Three questions guided this research

  1. Why did LGUs struggle to use the larger funds?
  2. Who reads the problem differently?
  3. Which solution best fits the least ready LGUs?

Source: MS2 Essay, Introduction.

What changed

The Supreme Court ruled that the LGU share is computed from all national taxes, not only those collected by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (DBM, 2021).

Executive Order 138 then required full devolution of basic services by the end of FY 2024, so national agencies began handing functions to LGUs (Office of the President of the Philippines, 2021).

What went wrong

The World Bank pointed to weak planning, thin staffing, limited financial management skills and procurement bottlenecks as reasons budgets went unspent ("WB Worried," 2021).

PIDS found wide variation in capacity. LGUs said full devolution by 2024 was out of reach, and provinces named hiring more personnel as an immediate need (Juco et al., 2024). Ateneo researchers likewise cite limited technical expertise and too few local human resources (Tuaño et al., 2026).

A note on the figures. The World Bank projected a 55 percent rise in the internal revenue allotment (World Bank, 2021b), while DBM reported a 37.89 percent rise in the FY 2022 allotment over the FY 2021 shares (DBM, 2021). The two likely differ because one is a pre-implementation projection and the other is the allotment DBM reported, so this site uses DBM's number.

EO 103 adds 3 to 4 years to the original FY 2024 deadline.

The problem, defined.

Larger local budgets arrived faster than many LGUs could plan, buy and spend, which weakens services and risks widening the gap between better-resourced and lower-income LGUs.

Scope

Provinces, cities and municipalities outside the Bangsamoro, with the focus on 4th to 6th class municipalities and their barangays. EO 103 gives priority to 4th and 5th class and other disadvantaged LGUs (PIA, 2025).

Time

From the FY 2022 allotment to the EO 103 deadlines of FY 2027 for cities and FY 2028 for provinces and municipalities.

Measures

Budget utilization, planning capacity, trained staff and shared arrangements, with the Seal of Good Local Governance and own-source revenue as context.

Root causes

Five root causesThree effects
  1. 1Capacity did not grow at the pace of funding
  2. 2One deadline for very unequal LGUs
  3. 3Planning treated as compliance
  4. 4Heavy dependence and upward accountability
  5. 5Support not shown to reach those who need it
The core problemMoney arrived faster than capacity
  • Unspent funds
  • Weaker services
  • Widening gaps

The evidence behind each cause, in the same order.

Capacity did not grow at the pace of funding

Weak planning, thin staffing, limited financial management skills and procurement bottlenecks held back spending ("WB Worried," 2021; Juco et al., 2026).

One deadline for very unequal LGUs

Capacity varied widely, and LGUs' own assessments showed full devolution by 2024 was out of reach (Juco et al., 2024).

Planning treated as compliance

A focus group study found transition plans were finished in a rush before the deadline (Titic, 2024).

Heavy dependence and upward accountability

Transfers made up 84 percent of municipal income on average in 2018, and accountability still runs mostly upward to the national government (Juco et al., 2026; "Philippine Devolution Still Lagging," 2026).

Support not shown to reach those who need it

Evidence on EO 103 support is early. DILG Region XI briefed its field officers (DILG Region XI, 2026), but I found no report yet of it reaching the 4th and 5th class LGUs, and the Growth Equity Fund was about 0.13 percent of the FY 2022 allotment (DBM, 2022).

Related issues Widening disparities between higher- and lower-income LGUs, unspent funds, and the upkeep of devolved health facilities, where most LGUs lack the budget (Juco et al., 2026).

How the problem was identified I combined national documents, research papers, peer-reviewed studies, news coverage and an interview with a barangay official, then checked each source for independence. Reading the evidence through three capacities, analytical, operational and political, is my own lens for separating root causes from symptoms.

Money needs three kinds of capacity.

A study of Indonesian local governments found that analytical, operational and political capacity had no reliable effect on sanitation services alone, but a significant effect together (Setiawan et al., 2022).

Each capacity alone showed no reliable effect. Service delivery sits where all three meet.

Analytical

Skilled staff and evidence-based policy. Thin planning figures, and transition plans treated as compliance, point here.

Operational

Finances, personnel and coordination. Weaker execution of capital-heavy budgets and procurement bottlenecks sit here.

Political

Stakeholder engagement and access to policymakers. The evidence is thin: one account that smaller barangays have less power to ask the city for help.

Sorting the Philippine evidence under these three headings is my own reading, not a finding of the Indonesian study, which covers only 2017 and 2018 and one service. Fixing procurement alone is unlikely to close the gap, though neither study tested that.

Funding still matters. Budget officers surveyed for DILG and UNDP ranked lack of investment funds first and lack of staff second ("Gov't Urged," 2022), so absorptive capacity is a constraint alongside funding, not instead of it.

Same pattern abroad

Three countries, one question: can capacity keep up?

1

Philippines

The ruling made the LGU share a slice of all national taxes. The allotment reached ₱959.04 billion in FY 2022, a 37.89 percent rise (DBM, 2021).

2

Indonesia

Its 2001 big bang decentralization moved about a third of central spending to the regions. Many local governments struggled to spend it, so money outran capacity (World Bank, 2007).

3

Colombia

Its 2001 reform made municipalities above 100,000 people autonomous in education. Smaller ones could be certified only if they met requirements, such as an aligned education plan and the capacity to run the sector (Elacqua et al., 2019).

Funding and capacity are two separate constraints.

Full actor list with roles

National government

  • Office of the PresidentIssued EO 138 and EO 103
  • Department of Budget and ManagementApproves transition plans, runs the Growth Equity Fund
  • Department of FinanceBureau of Local Government Finance monitors LGU finances
  • DILG and Local Government AcademyLead capacity development and run EO 103 orientations in the regions (DILG Region XI, 2026)

  • Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS)A government research institute that recommends asymmetric decentralization

  • Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)Guidance on capacity building and incremental approaches (OECD, 2019)

Where they disagree

DBM
Fiscal stability. Wants devolved functions handed over fully and permanently, though gradually (DBM, 2021). Even inside DBM, an undersecretary said in 2022 that big ticket infrastructure functions should wait until 2025 to 2027 ("Experts Push," 2022).
Dept. of Finance
Frames it as a spending problem. In 2023 the Finance Secretary asked the President to encourage LGUs to use more of what they receive ("Diokno Asks Marcos," 2023).
DILG
Caution. Recommended that phasing account for institutional and fiscal capacity (Juco et al., 2026).
LGUs and ULAP
Their own assessments showed full devolution by 2024 was out of reach. ULAP proposed shifting from devolution to a service delivery enhancement framework (Juco et al., 2024; ULAP, 2023).
PIDS and World Bank
Capacity and equity. They recommend asymmetric decentralization and a capacity-based review of re-devolved functions (Juco et al., 2024; PIDS, 2023a; World Bank, 2021b).

How the sources were weighed DBM's FAQ describes its own policy, not an outside assessment. PIDS is a government research institute, so its findings are informed but not fully independent. The World Bank figures were projections made before implementation, and ULAP is an advocacy body. A scoping review of ten studies cannot prove cause (Andaya et al., 2026).

Section 3 of 9 · Source: Essay only

Media Presentation

How the news and one barangay account framed the ruling.

How the news told it.

Coverage keeps pairing good news with a warning. Bigger budgets are announced, then capacity is questioned.

2021

The World Bank warns that unspent funds could reach ₱155 billion in 2022, a forecast and not a result ("WB Worried," 2021).

March 2023

The President suspends EO 138 and orders a review. DILG recommends phasing that accounts for LGU capacity (Juco et al., 2026).

November 6, 2025

EO 103 extends the transition, with deadlines tied to differing LGU capabilities and priority for poorer localities (Hufana, 2025; Romero, 2025).

March 2026

DBM confirms that the Growth Equity Fund continues (DBM, 2026).

June 2026

PIDS reports that devolution remains incomplete despite higher funding (Juco et al., 2026; Manila Bulletin Newsroom, 2026).

National agencies, researchers and planners are heard far more than municipal or barangay officials and residents. Local voices appear mostly through ULAP (ULAP, 2023). Regional planners were more upbeat, saying the larger share would help LGUs attract investment ("Mandanas Ruling Seen," 2023).

From a barangay A Sangguniang Kabataan chairman in Barangay Landayan, San Pedro, Laguna said procurement is the bottleneck, since bidding, paperwork and audit review stall projects while many officials remain untrained. In floods the barangay clears canals and evacuates residents first but lacks equipment and engineers, and often waits on the city. He said it is better to move slowly and get it right. This is one interested view and an illustration, not proof, paraphrased from an interview in Filipino (J. Anaya, personal communication, September 29, 2026).

Defining Solutions

Three solutions: what each aims to do, how it works and where it falls short.

Core 3 of 5Three solutions

Three ways to close the gap.

The highest scoring option becomes the base of the proposal. Tap a panel to open it for its aim, how it works, its best aspect and where it falls short.

Rank 1 · Selected as the base

EO 103 phased devolution

3.4out of 4

Moves functions as LGUs become ready, with priority help for 4th and 5th class and disadvantaged LGUs. Already in force, with clear deadlines.

Gap: only early orientations, with no report yet of support reaching the 4th and 5th class LGUs.

Open details +
Aim
Move functions as LGUs become ready, with priority help for 4th and 5th class and disadvantaged LGUs (PIA, 2025).
How it works
DBM reviews agency transition plans, the Local Government Academy builds capacity, and the Bureau of Local Government Finance monitors.
Best aspect
Readiness checklists in the transition plans make readiness a gate, and differentiated pacing matches OECD guidance on asymmetric arrangements (Allain-Dupré et al., 2020; OECD, 2019).
Main challenge
More time does not build capacity by itself, and capacity building needs long-term commitment (OECD, 2019). The evidence is early: DILG Region XI briefed its field officers in June 2026 (DILG Region XI, 2026), but I found no report yet of support reaching the 4th and 5th class LGUs.
Rank 2

Growth Equity Fund

2.8out of 4

Tops up poorer LGUs. In the proposal, releases follow capacity milestones.

Open details +
Aim
Top up the allotment of poor LGUs that cannot fund devolved services.
How it works
DBM releases money to eligible LGUs by poverty incidence and per capita allotment. The FY 2022 round was ₱1.25 billion (DBM, 2022). It covered three provinces, 150 municipalities and 270 isolated barangays, and the FY 2023 round covered 70 municipalities and 100 barangays (DBM, 2022, 2024).
Best aspect
Allocation follows a formula, and utilization is reported quarterly.
Main challenge
It is about 0.13 percent of the FY 2022 allotment and cannot pay for salaries or training (DBM, 2021, 2022, 2024).
Rank 3

Inter-LGU alliances

2.4out of 4

Pools professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff. In the proposal, provinces anchor the pools.

Open details +
Aim
Let neighboring LGUs share professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff that none could afford alone, under Section 33 of the Local Government Code.
How it works
Members sign agreements and contribute shares, as in the bay alliances of Northern Mindanao and the Surallah landfill cluster in South Cotabato.
Best aspect
Clear written agreements and provincial support, as when Surallah's trained engineer later designed a landfill cell alone (Ballesteros et al., 2023).
Main challenge
Weak contracts and unpaid shares. Only 28 of 327 sanitary landfill sites were shared by more than one LGU in 2022. In a review of 40 marine protected area alliances, only about 24 percent were active (Horigue et al., 2012), a different sector and so a rough warning.

What a readiness gate could look like

Colombia offers the nearest model. Smaller municipalities there had to meet requirements, such as an aligned education plan and the institutional capacity to run the sector, before taking over education, and the department decided whether they had (Elacqua et al., 2019). That is close to what EO 103 asks of agencies through transition plans and readiness checklists, and the assessor sat one tier above the municipality and not at the center. The combined proposal gives provinces a similar middle role, as anchors of shared staff and not as certifiers.

Three things do not carry over. The 100,000 line was a population rule and not a measure of capacity, the case covers one sector while devolution here spans many, and only the design of the certification is used, not how certified municipalities performed.

At the barangay level, a Sangguniang Kabataan chairman's test is that a barangay is ready when it has trained budgeting and procurement staff, a professional in their respective field, and clear responsibility for each task (J. Anaya, personal communication, September 29, 2026). An LGU that falls short could draw on an alliance for shared professionals in their respective fields until it passes, since the Growth Equity Fund cannot pay for salaries or training (DBM, 2022, 2024).

The barangay test is one interested view, not proof.

Why each score

From the Week 8 worksheet, one rater's reasons for each SMART score.

EO 103 phased devolution (3.4)
  • Specific, 3: Clear on who (all LGUs except the Bangsamoro), what (phased devolution) and priority groups, but it does not itself define how capacity is built.
  • Measurable, 2: Requires results based monitoring and fiscal monitoring, but sets no indicators or targets, and PIDS says earlier indicator systems lacked credibility.
  • Attainable, 4: Already signed and in force, with machinery in place (transition plans, Local Government Academy, Bureau of Local Government Finance).
  • Relevant, 4: Directly answers the problem, devolution moving faster than readiness.
  • Time-based, 4: FY 2027 for cities, FY 2028 for provinces and municipalities, and 15 day and 90 day steps for agencies.
Growth Equity Fund (2.8)
  • Specific, 3: Eligible LGUs and criteria are defined (poverty incidence, per capita allotment), but it targets the funding gap and not the capacity gap.
  • Measurable, 3: Quarterly utilization reports track disbursement and completion, but I found no compiled results.
  • Attainable, 3: The fund exists and continues, but it is small (₱1.25 billion in FY 2022), cannot pay salaries or training, and needs a submitted transition plan.
  • Relevant, 2: Supports poor LGUs, but contributes only indirectly to closing the capacity gap.
  • Time-based, 3: Time bound release and quarterly reporting, ending when a fiscal equalization grant replaces it, though milestones are not specific.
Inter-LGU alliances (2.4)
  • Specific, 3: The idea is specific (shared professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff for neighboring lower-income LGUs), but Section 33 is general and the verified examples are in other sectors.
  • Measurable, 2: Possible indicators exist (alliances still active, cost savings, service coverage), but there is no baseline for shared technical staff.
  • Attainable, 3: Section 33 gives the legal basis, but weak contracts, insufficient funds and dependence on leaders are common obstacles.
  • Relevant, 3: Pooled staff address the capacity gap directly, but say little about the pace of devolution.
  • Time-based, 1: No timeframe or deadline for forming or reviewing alliances is provided.
SMART profile, scale 1 to 4

EO 103 scores highest on attainable, relevant and time-based. The Growth Equity Fund is weakest on relevance, and inter-LGU alliances on time-based. These are one rater's scores. Tap a name to isolate its shape.

Not a fourth entry. Scored on the same five SMART criteria as the three solutions above, the combined proposal also lands at 3.4 (Effective), level with EO 103 alone and not above it. It gains on Specific and Measurable and gives up some Attainable and Time-based, because the shared staff part is untried, uncosted and has no deadline. The dashed outline marks a design that has not been tried anywhere. These are one rater's scores.

Why these five scores
  • Specific, 4: Five actions, each with an owner, a fallback and a scope (4th to 6th class municipalities).
  • Measurable, 3: Six indicators, five with a baseline, but no numeric targets and no baseline yet for trained staff.
  • Attainable, 3: EO 103 is in force and the fund exists, but shared staff is untried, uncosted and depends on provinces that may lack professionals in their respective fields.
  • Relevant, 4: Answers both the pace of devolution and the capacity gap directly.
  • Time-based, 3: EO 103 deadlines (FY 2027 and FY 2028) and an annual review, but no dated step for forming the sharing agreements.

How the solution was chosen.

Each move narrowed the options. Swipe or scroll sideways.

Collect candidates

Three options came from the research: EO 103 phased deadlines, the Growth Equity Fund and inter-LGU alliances.

Score each one

Each was rated 1 to 4 on the five SMART criteria. EO 103 ranked first at 3.4.

Read the gaps

EO 103's support has only begun, with orientations and no report yet of it reaching the neediest LGUs. The fund is small and cannot pay for staff. Alliances have a mixed record (Ferrer et al., 2018).

Combine the parts

EO 103 became the base, with milestone-based fund releases and province-anchored shared staff added where it is weakest.

Test for failure

Costs, failure conditions and a fallback were written down before choosing, and six indicators were set to test the design.

First place was not enough, so the answer is a combination.

Section 6 of 9 · Source: Worksheet and Essay

Validating the Solution and the Combined Proposal

The combined proposal, who owns each step and what happens if a step fails.

Pace by readiness, with help where it is thinnest.

EO 103 is the base. The fund and shared staff cover where it is weakest.

  1. Approve transition plansAgencies submit plans with readiness checklists, and DBM reviews them.
  2. Build capacity where it is thinnestThe Local Government Academy trains budgeting and procurement staff, starting with 4th and 5th class LGUs.
  3. Release funds against milestonesGrowth Equity Fund money follows capacity milestones, not plan submission alone.
  4. Share professionals across municipalitiesProvinces anchor pools of staff through written agreements that state each member's share and penalties.
  5. Track six indicatorsReview them every year until FY 2028, reported separately for 4th to 6th class municipalities.

Numbers match the five actions above. The combination is my own design and has not been tried anywhere.

What is new

A province anchors Section 33 pools of shared professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff for neighboring lower-income municipalities, which is where PIDS sees provinces as indispensable (PIDS, 2023b). A city or municipality writes its barangays into the agreement, so a barangay holds a standing claim and not a request that waits in line. Fund releases follow capacity milestones, not plan submission alone.

This combination is my own design and has not been tried anywhere. South Cotabato shows a small version, where Surallah's trained engineer later designed a landfill cell alone (Ballesteros et al., 2023).

Real-world factors

Each member pays its own share from its own allotment, as the written agreement states. I found no costing for shared staff, and the fund cannot pay for salaries or training (DBM, 2022, 2024). The pools hold only if each share is written down, penalties are enforced and no single source carries the funding.

The bigger risk is the province itself, since provinces named hiring more personnel as an immediate need (Juco et al., 2024). The fallback is for the Local Government Academy and national capacity building bodies to lend technical staff until the province can anchor on its own. That adds a national cost.

Where this stands in real lifeThe fund has grown a lot since the FY 2022 round used above. The FY 2026 appropriation is ₱11.3 billion, about nine times the ₱1.25 billion of FY 2022. It goes straight to mostly 4th and 5th class LGUs in fixed amounts: ₱100 million for the province, ₱75 million for each city, ₱30 million for each municipality and about ₱3.9 million for each barangay (DBM, 2026). It is not released against capacity milestones, since LGUs submit their documents after the money arrives (DBM, 2026). The bar on capacity building, administrative expenses and personnel costs still holds, so the fund still cannot pay for shared staff (DBM, 2026). The same circular tells LGUs to seek technical help from the next higher LGU, such as a municipality from its province (DBM, 2026), a small real-life version of province anchoring. Action 3, tying releases to milestones, is therefore still my own proposal and not current practice.

Fitting each solution to the Philippines, and who to tap

Source: Week 8 Worksheet, customizing the solution to the Philippine setting.

Solution 1

EO 103 phased devolution

Keep EO 103 as the base and make the readiness gate concrete, for example that an LGU has trained budgeting and procurement staff, a professional in their respective field and clear responsibility for each task, an idea drawn from Colombia. An LGU that falls short can draw on shared professionals in their respective fields until it passes.

Who to tap. DBM, DILG and the Local Government Academy, the DOF Bureau of Local Government Finance, ULAP, provincial governments, 4th to 6th class municipalities and barangay officials.

Solution 2

Growth Equity Fund

Release funds in tranches tied to capacity milestones in each LGU's transition plan, not plan submission alone. Because the fund cannot pay for salaries or training, staff sharing is funded by members' own allotment shares.

Who to tap. DBM, the Bureau of the Treasury, the inter-agency steering committee (DBM, DILG, DOF and the national planning agency), eligible LGUs and PIDS for evaluation.

Solution 3

Inter-LGU alliances

Provinces anchor Section 33 pools of shared professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff for neighboring lower-income municipalities. Written agreements state each member's share, responsibilities and penalties for breach, and a city or municipality writes its barangays into the agreement. Where a province lacks professionals in their respective fields, the Local Government Academy and national capacity building bodies lend technical staff until it can anchor on its own.

Who to tap. Provincial governments, city and municipal councils (which approve the agreements), barangays, DILG and the Local Government Academy, DBM, ULAP and private sector partners where joint ventures make sense.

Who owns each step, and what if it fails.

Every action has a named owner and a fallback, so the plan does not depend on everything going right.

Action
Owner
What could go wrong
Contingency
1. Approve transition plans
OwnerDBM, national agencies and LGUs.
What could go wrongPlans become a compliance exercise (Titic, 2024).
ContingencyTie fund releases to capacity milestones, not plan submission alone.
2. Build capacity
OwnerDILG through the Local Government Academy, with the DOF Bureau of Local Government Finance.
What could go wrongSupport is underfunded or never reaches LGUs.
ContingencyShow capacity funding as its own line in agency proposals and track trained staff by income class.
3. Release funds against milestones
OwnerDBM, the Bureau of the Treasury and the steering committee of DBM, DILG, DOF and the national planning agency.
What could go wrongThe fund has grown but is still not released against milestones and cannot pay salaries or training (DBM, 2022, 2024, 2026).
ContingencyDo not count on it for staff. Members pay their shares from their own allotment.
4. Share professionals
OwnerProvincial governments, city and municipal councils and member LGUs, with the Local Government Academy as fallback.
What could go wrongAn alliance goes quiet through weak contracts, unpaid shares or new leaders, or the province has no professionals in their respective fields (Ferrer et al., 2018; Juco et al., 2024).
ContingencyEnforce penalties, avoid a single funding source, get provincial and national backing, and borrow national staff until the province can anchor. That adds a national cost I have not costed.
5. Track six indicators
OwnerBureau of Local Government Finance, DILG and DBM, with PIDS for evaluation.
What could go wrongIndicators lack credibility or baselines.
ContingencyKeep to six indicators built on data agencies already hold, and treat the first count as the baseline.

The smaller tasks behind each action

Task 1 supports action 1, task 2 action 2, and so on.

  1. Agencies form devolution transition committees within 15 days and submit plans within 90 days after the implementing rules take effect, with readiness criteria included. LGUs update their plans to the extended timeline (Philippine News Agency, 2025; Romero, 2025).
  2. Local Government Academy training in public financial management, local planning, investment programming, budgeting and revenue generation. A first count of trained budgeting and procurement staff sets the baseline, and capacity building funding goes into FY 2027 agency proposals.
  3. Set capacity milestones in each LGU's transition plan. The steering committee checks them before release, and quarterly utilization reports follow.
  4. Neighboring LGUs agree on shares. Councils approve a Memorandum of Agreement stating contributions, responsibilities and penalties. A city or municipality writes its barangays in, and the province assigns or hires the professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff.
  5. Collect data agencies already hold, compile baselines, report by income class and hold the annual review.

Do the owners agree?

Mostly. DBM wants devolved functions turned over fully but gradually, and EO 103 keeps full devolution with new deadlines. DILG, LGUs, ULAP, PIDS and the World Bank all want capacity in place before functions move down.

The friction points are real. DBM has limited fiscal space for capacity funding, many provinces lack personnel, and cities must be willing to write barangays into agreements. ULAP also proposed replacing devolution with a service delivery enhancement approach, while this proposal keeps devolution.

Laws and resources to lean on

The Mandanas-Garcia ruling (final April 10, 2019), EO 138 (2021) as amended by EO 103 (2025), and the Local Government Code, including Section 17 on devolved functions, Section 33 on cooperative undertakings and Section 284 on the 40 percent LGU share (Local Government Code of 1991, 1991). DBM National Budget Memorandum No. 157 and Local Budget Circulars 146 and 159 cover the fund.

The Seal of Good Local Governance and its Performance Challenge Fund reward strong performers. The Local Government Academy's segmentation rated 534 of 1,698 LGUs low on both capacity and performance (Local Government Academy, 2024), which shows where to start.

Core 4 of 5Call to action

What to do next.

The proposal only works if the people who own each step act on it. Each owner already named in this site has one clear move to make now.

1. DBM and agencies

DBM, national agencies and LGUs approve transition plans that carry readiness criteria and tie fund releases to capacity milestones so a plan on paper is not mistaken for readiness.

2. DILG and the Academy

DILG, through the Local Government Academy and with the Bureau of Local Government Finance, delivers training in budgeting, planning and procurement and shows capacity building as its own line in FY 2027 agency proposals.

3. DBM and Treasury

DBM, the Bureau of the Treasury and the steering committee release Growth Equity Fund money against capacity milestones, and do not count on it to pay for staff.

4. Provinces and LGUs

Provincial governments, councils and member LGUs sign sharing agreements that state each member's contribution, responsibilities and penalties, write barangays in, and let the province anchor the shared professionals in their respective fields and procurement staff.

5. BLGF, DILG, DBM, PIDS

The Bureau of Local Government Finance, DILG, DBM and PIDS take the first count, then publish the six indicators every year by income class, so success is judged by results and not announcements.

The ask in one line Pace the handover by readiness, and put help where it is thinnest first.

Judge it by results, not announcements.

08

Core 5 of 5Conclusion

Section 8 of 9 · Source: Essay only

Conclusion

Where the case lands. It covers the assessment of the solution, questions you might ask and what the case means for decentralization theory and the SDGs.

Assessing the solution.

Success is judged by results and not announcements. Four indicators track the proposal directly: spending, planning, trained staff and shared arrangements. Two are context measures that show the trend but cannot show the proposal caused it.

How success is measured Indicators are reviewed annually until FY 2028 and reported separately for 4th to 6th class municipalities. Where no baseline exists, the first count becomes it. Progress means rising above each baseline while narrowing the gap with higher-class LGUs, and a rise that reaches only the stronger LGUs would not count. I left out the completion speed of fund projects and the per capita cost of shared services because they have no baseline or public source.

Challenges encountered
  • Evidence on EO 103 support is early, with orientations but no report yet of capacity building or funds reaching 4th and 5th class LGUs, and no costing for shared professionals in their respective fields or procurement staff.
  • Several baselines are thin or missing, including trained staff and shared arrangements.
  • Key sources are not fully independent: PIDS is a government research institute, and DBM describes its own policy.
  • Some evidence is small or narrow, such as 11 municipalities in Masbate (Laurio & Malto, 2023) and one service in Indonesia over 2017 and 2018.
  • The interview is one interested view, and the scores come from one rater.
Opportunities for improvement
  • Put the costing question to a provincial planning office or the Local Government Academy.
  • Take the first count of trained budgeting and procurement staff.
  • Compile results from the Growth Equity Fund rounds.
  • Interview more LGUs, especially smaller municipalities, and have several raters score the options.
Recommendations for future implementation
  • Write each member's share, responsibilities and penalties into every sharing agreement, and enforce them (Ferrer et al., 2018; Juco et al., 2026).
  • Never let a single source carry the funding of a shared pool.
  • Tie Growth Equity Fund releases to capacity milestones.
  • Publish indicator results every year by income class.
Long-term implications
  • If capacity grows alongside funding, LGUs can lean less on transfers and the promise of Target 16.6 can reach residents.
  • If not, health coverage may follow a municipality's income class: the rise in health spending was meaningful in first class municipalities but only marginal in fifth and sixth class ones (Juco et al., 2026). Nisperos et al. (2024) likewise note that full devolution of health services raises urgent concerns about continuity of care.

What the process taught

Two separate constraints

Elsewhere the usual complaint is a lack of money (Marta et al., 2024), but here administrative capacity became a constraint once the money arrived.

First place is not enough

EO 103 ranked first, yet its support is not yet shown to reach the neediest LGUs, so the answer became a combination.

A score is not proof

The combined design is my own rating of something untried, which is why the indicators exist.

Sources need weighing

Several key sources were not fully independent, so each was read for what it can and cannot show.

At a glance

The conclusion in four boxes.

ChallengesEarly and thin evidence

EO 103 support early, thin baselines, sources not fully independent, one rater.

ImproveFour next steps

Cost shared staff, count trained staff, compile fund results, interview more LGUs.

RecommendFour rules

Write and enforce shares, no single funder, milestone releases, yearly results by income class.

Long-termTwo paths

If capacity grows, less reliance on transfers. If not, health coverage may follow income class.

Questions you might ask.

Why not just give LGUs more money?

Funding still matters, but budget officers ranked lack of investment funds first and lack of staff second ("Gov't Urged," 2022). Money without staff to plan and buy leaves funds unspent.

Why not delay devolution for everyone?

EO 103 already extends the deadlines, but a longer timeline does not build capacity by itself, so support has to come with it.

Why not use the Growth Equity Fund alone?

It was about 0.13 percent of the FY 2022 allotment and cannot pay for salaries or training (DBM, 2022, 2024).

Is the combined proposal proven?

No. It is my design and has not been tried anywhere, so six indicators are set to test it.

How is this different from ULAP's proposal?

ULAP proposed shifting from devolution to a service delivery enhancement approach (ULAP, 2023). This proposal keeps devolution and paces it by readiness.

Whose view is missing?

Municipal and barangay officials and residents are heard far less. One barangay interview is used as an illustration, not as proof.

Why it matters beyond one ruling.

A test of decentralization theory

The classical case says welfare is at least as high when local public goods are provided locally, since government sits closer to the people. It assumes the closer level can actually deliver. This case tests that assumption (Oates, 1972, 1999, as cited in Setiawan et al., 2022).

Links to the global goals

It bears on SDG Target 16.6, effective institutions at all levels (United Nations, 2026a). Its indicator 16.6.1 asks how closely governments spend what their approved budgets planned, but when the report was written it covered only central government, so it does not show what happens in LGUs (International Budget Partnership, 2023). It also bears on health services (Target 3.8, universal health coverage, United Nations, 2026b), since most LGUs lack the budget to maintain devolved health facilities (Juco et al., 2026; Manila Bulletin Newsroom, 2026). Success should be judged by results and not announcements.

Section 9 of 9 · Source: Worksheet and Essay

Terms, Limits and Sources

Key terms, the limits of the evidence and the full reference list.

Terms, limits and sources.

Devolution. Moving functions and funds from national agencies to local governments.

National Tax Allotment. The share of national taxes that goes to LGUs, set at 40 percent.

Absorptive capacity. An LGU's ability to turn money into services through planning, staffing and procurement.

Limits. There is no costing for shared staff, and the scores come from one rater. Evidence on EO 103 support is early: DILG Region XI briefed its field officers on the order in June 2026 (DILG Region XI, 2026), but I found no report yet of capacity building or funds reaching the 4th and 5th class LGUs it prioritizes.
